name: Textual
vendor: Will McGugan and contributors (built at Textualize, Inc. until mid-2025)
summary: A Python framework for terminal apps with a widget tree, CSS-style stylesheets and asyncio event handling, built on the Rich library; the same app can also be served to a web browser.
intro: Textual is retained mode, closer to a web page than a drawing API. An app subclasses `App` and yields widgets from `compose()`; they form a DOM-like tree under a `Screen`. Styles live in Textual CSS (`.tcss` files or a `CSS` string) with type, id and class selectors and rules such as `dock: top`; unlike browser CSS, a type selector also matches subclasses. Events and messages are handled by methods named `on_<event>`, and each widget is powered by its own task on Python’s asyncio, with input arriving as events on the app’s message queue. Reactive attributes refresh a widget automatically when they change, batching several changes into one repaint, and the Worker API moves slow work such as network calls off the message loop so the UI stays responsive.

Under the hood, widgets render to Rich segments (runs of text with one style). A compositor cuts the segments of overlapping widgets into equal-width “chops”, keeps the top-most ones and writes a single stream of escape codes, updating only the regions that changed. A spatial map on a grid of 100 by 20 cells lets it skip widgets scrolled out of view, so finding the visible ones takes about as long for 1,000 widgets as for 8. Apps can take over the screen or run inline below the prompt, and `textual-serve` runs an app on a server and streams it over a WebSocket to xterm.js in a browser.

Will McGugan, the author of Rich, started Textual in 2021 and founded Textualize, Inc. to work on it full time. In May 2025 the company announced it would wrap up because it hadn’t found a viable business; Textual continues as an MIT-licensed open-source project. It is still maintained, almost entirely by McGugan: version 8.2.8 shipped in June 2026 and commits landed in October 2026.
strengths: Web-style development in Python: a widget tree, CSS that restyles built-in and third-party widgets, and live reloading of styles with `textual run my_app.py --dev`
Ready-made widgets, from a basic button to a syntax-highlighted `TextArea`, with keyboard and mouse input handled for you
Concurrency fits Python’s asyncio: handlers can be `async`, and workers keep slow I/O from freezing the interface
One codebase for terminal and browser: through `textual-serve`, `App.open_url` and `App.deliver_text` work in both
limits: Its company is gone: since Textualize closed in mid-2025, development depends mostly on one maintainer’s time
Frequent major versions: 1.0 arrived in December 2024 and 8.0 in February 2026, so upgrades need care
Needs Python 3.9 or later (3.10 for the tree-sitter syntax highlighting extras), and a terminal with more than 256 colors looks much better; macOS’s default Terminal is limited to 256
In the browser the app still runs on the server as a subprocess of `textual-serve`, with the terminal drawn by xterm.js: it is not a static web app

story: Will McGugan first wrote Rich, a Python library for colored and formatted terminal output, as a hobby project, then asked why not build an application framework on top of it. Textual’s first release, 0.1.0, went to PyPI in June 2021. The terminal offered only the basics (move the cursor, write colored text, read keys and mouse movements), so everything from a button to a text editor had to be built from scratch.

McGugan founded Textualize, Inc. and worked on Textual full time with a small team. By late 2021 the framework took its styling from CSS, separating an app’s layout and design from its logic. Later work added inline apps, serving apps to web browsers, and in December 2024 a 1.0 release.

In May 2025 McGugan announced that Textualize would wrap up within weeks: Textual had been “a solution in search of a problem”, and the team hadn’t found a shared pain point to build a business around. Textual became a community project, still maintained by McGugan, who then built Toad (“Textual Code”), a terminal front end for AI coding agents, on top of it.

choices.why: Keeping styles out of Python avoids tangled UI code, lets developers restyle built-in and third-party widgets as easily as their own, and makes live editing of the design possible.

Treating the screen as a 2D array of characters breaks down with double-width characters such as emoji and Asian scripts. Working with Rich’s styled segments, and splitting them into chops, made overlapping widgets tractable.
Every widget is powered by an async task and handlers can be coroutines, so an app can await network libraries such as httpx, and workers run slow jobs without blocking the UI.

choices.choice: Serve the terminal protocol to browsers
choices.why: Rather than a separate web renderer, `textual-serve` pipes the app’s escape codes over a WebSocket to xterm.js, with extra APIs for links and file downloads, so one app works in a terminal and a browser.

timeline.text: Textual 0.1.0 published on PyPI (June); Textual CSS in development (November)
Browser features for apps served with textual-serve (September)
Textualize, the company, announces it will wrap up; Textual continues as open source (May)
McGugan releases Toad, built on Textual (December)
